cards.front: What two questions sort a Claude use case into go, go-with-safeguards, or don't?
cards.back: **If it's wrong, who is hurt and how badly?** and **Will a capable person review it before anyone acts on it?**

cards.front: Name four tasks that are a good fit for Claude with light review.
cards.back: Drafting, summarizing, brainstorming, rewriting for a new audience. Analysis and research also fit, provided a person reviews and verifies the result.

cards.front: Which high-risk use-case areas does Anthropic's Usage Policy name?
cards.back: Legal, healthcare, insurance, finance, employment and housing, academic testing and admissions, and media or journalism.

cards.front: What two safeguards does the Usage Policy expect for high-risk uses that reach consumers?
cards.back: **Human-in-the-loop**: a qualified professional in that field reviews the content. **Disclosure**: people are told AI is involved.

cards.front: What must every consumer-facing chatbot disclose under the Usage Policy?
cards.back: That users are interacting with an AI, not a human (at minimum at the start of each chat session).

cards.front: Can a prohibited use under the Usage Policy be made acceptable with human review?
cards.back: No. Prohibited uses are off-limits whatever safeguards you add. Review and disclosure apply to **high-risk** uses, not prohibited ones.

cards.front: A manager wants Claude to auto-reject the bottom half of applicants. How do you redesign it?
cards.back: Claude summarizes each application against stated job-related criteria. A recruiter or hiring manager makes every decision.

cards.front: Is a disclaimer such as 'AI-generated, may contain errors' a substitute for review?
cards.back: No. A disclaimer shifts the burden to the reader. High-stakes output still needs a qualified human to check it.

cards.front: List four signals that a task needs extra safeguards.
cards.back: It reaches customers, regulators or the public. It contains numbers, legal, medical or citation content someone will rely on. It decides or ranks people. It will be published automatically.

cards.front: What are typical data classes to check before using Claude?
cards.back: Public, internal, confidential, and regulated or personal (such as health, financial, payroll, student records, customer identifiers).

cards.front: What are the three moves for handling sensitive data with Claude?
cards.back: **Minimize** (only what the task needs), **de-identify** (remove or replace identifiers), and **use the approved channel** (the company workspace and plan).

cards.front: Why is 'tell Claude not to remember this' not a data control?
cards.back: It is a request to the model, not a change to storage or policy. The data has already been shared, and policy decides whether it may be shared at all.

cards.front: What is an indirect identifier? Give an example.
cards.back: Details that identify someone without a name, such as 'the only female engineer in the Leeds office' or a rare job title plus a date.

cards.front: Give three ways to de-identify a spreadsheet before analysis.
cards.back: Replace names with codes, drop or mask account numbers and contact details, and generalize (an age band instead of a date of birth, a region instead of an address).

cards.front: At the time of writing, are inputs to commercial plans (Team, Enterprise, API) used to train Anthropic models by default?
cards.back: No, not by default, per the Anthropic Privacy Center (explicit feedback such as thumbs up/down is an exception). Consumer plans (Free, Pro, Max) have a 'help improve Claude' setting.

cards.front: Why use the company workspace instead of a personal Claude account for work data?
cards.back: The organization chose that plan's data terms, admin controls and policies. Personal accounts fall outside those controls and usually break the approved-tools rule.

cards.front: What's the difference between pausing and resetting Claude's memory?
cards.back: **Pause** keeps existing memories but stops new ones. **Reset** permanently deletes all memories and can't be undone.

cards.front: How does memory work across Projects?
cards.back: Each Project has its own separate memory space and summary, so context stays focused and separate between Projects.

cards.front: What do incognito chats do, and what don't they do?
cards.back: They aren't saved to chat history or used by memory. They **don't** make it acceptable to share data your policy forbids.

cards.front: Who controls memory availability on Team and Enterprise plans?
cards.back: Organization owners (Owners and Primary Owners) in organization settings.

cards.front: Why are connectors a governance consideration?
cards.back: They let Claude read from tools such as email, drives and calendars, which widens what can enter a conversation. Connect only what the task needs and only approved connectors.

cards.front: What should you do right after realizing you shared sensitive data by mistake?
cards.back: Report it promptly through your organization's incident or data-protection channel and follow its guidance. Don't just delete the chat and stay silent.

cards.front: Your AI policy is silent on a data type you want to use. What do you do?
cards.back: Ask the policy owner (security, legal, compliance or HR) before you proceed. Don't assume, and don't ask Claude to interpret the policy.

cards.front: A faster workaround exists outside approved tools. Should you use it?
cards.back: No. Follow the policy and request a review of the tool or feature you need through the proper owner.

cards.front: Which requests should an Associate escalate rather than build?
cards.back: Integrations with business systems, automated pipelines, API builds and agents that act on systems. Route them to governance owners and to Developers or Architects.

cards.front: Name the five ethical principles from this domain.
cards.back: Accountability, transparency, fairness, privacy and consent, and human judgment (avoiding overreliance).

cards.front: Who is accountable for an error in AI-assisted work you sent?
cards.back: You and your organization. 'Claude wrote it' is never a defense.

cards.front: When should you disclose AI assistance?
cards.back: When policy, law or audience expectations call for it, such as client deliverables, published content, education settings or consumer chatbots. When in doubt, disclose.

cards.front: Three practical bias checks for content that affects people?
cards.back: Give neutral, job-relevant criteria. Ask Claude to flag biased or exclusionary language. Compare outputs across cases that should be treated alike.

cards.front: What are signs of overreliance on AI?
cards.back: Approving outputs without reading them in full, being unable to explain your own document, and juniors never practising core skills.

cards.front: Name two intellectual-property habits for AI-assisted work.
cards.back: Don't upload material you lack rights to use that way, and verify and attribute sources rather than presenting copied or AI-written text as your own where it matters.

cards.front: What are the four answer types in governance questions, and which usually wins?
cards.back: Ignore the risk, ask the model to behave, abandon the task, and **enable safely**. Enable safely usually wins.

cards.front: When is 'abandon the task' the right answer?
cards.back: Only when the use is prohibited by the Usage Policy or your organization's policy, or when no safeguard could make it acceptable.

cards.front: In a 'choose two' governance item, what does the correct pair usually look like?
cards.back: Two complementary real safeguards, for example 'remove identifiers' plus 'use the approved workspace', or 'qualified review' plus 'disclose AI use'.

cards.front: Does deadline pressure or a senior requester justify skipping review?
cards.back: No. Urgency and seniority never override data, review or disclosure controls.
